notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of set bits for every integer from zero through n.
Idea: Use the largest power of two not exceeding each i to split it into a power and remainder.
Technique and why it applies: The code computes exponent with logarithms, sets num=2^exponent, and adds dp[num]+dp[i%num] unless i itself is a power of two.
Invariant: The recurrence counts the set bit in the highest power plus the bits in the lower remainder.
Edge cases: Floating logarithms may misidentify powers near precision boundaries; math is not imported in the snippet.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output storage; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return bit counts for every integer from zero through num.
Idea: Build each answer from the count for its right-shifted half plus its low bit.
Technique and why it applies: res[i] is (i&1)+res[i>>1], reusing the already computed value for floor(i/2).
Invariant: The recurrence removes the least significant bit and adds one when that bit is set.
Edge cases: num=0 returns [0]; the result list includes all values through num.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Check whether a positive integer is a power of four.
Idea: Take its base-four logarithm and test whether the result is integral.
Technique and why it applies: The code rejects nonpositive values, then calls math.log(n,4).is_integer().
Invariant: Powers of four have integer logarithms, while other positive integers do not mathematically.
Edge cases: Floating-point rounding can make exact-integrality tests unreliable for large inputs.
Complexity: O(1) time and space in the arithmetic model; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether num is a power of four.
Idea: Repeatedly shift right by two bits while the low two bits are zero.
Technique and why it applies: The loop removes factors of four; the final value must be exactly one.
Invariant: Only numbers with a leading one and all other bits zero at even positions reduce to one.
Edge cases: Zero exits the loop and fails the final comparison; negative inputs also fail.
Complexity: O(log n) loop iterations in general, not O(1) asymptotically; O(1) space. Author time label is questionable.

Task and constraints: Check whether an integer is a power of four using its binary representation.
Idea: Inspect the binary string's leading bit, length, and zero count.
Technique and why it applies: The code requires a leading one, compares bit-string length with total zero count, requires an odd zero count, and rejects a minus sign.
Invariant: A power of four has one set bit at an even exponent, but the implemented length/zero-count condition does not correctly encode that property.
Edge cases: For example, 16's binary representation fails the length-equals-zero-count test, so this implementation is incorrect.
Complexity: Time and space are O(log n) due to string conversion; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether num is a power of four using bit operations.
Idea: Require positivity, a single set bit, and that bit to lie in an allowed position.
Technique and why it applies: The first bit test checks power-of-two form; the mask 0b0101... requires the set bit to occupy an even binary position.
Invariant: A valid power of four has exactly one set bit among the mask's permitted positions.
Edge cases: Zero and negatives are rejected; the fixed mask covers the stated integer range.
Complexity: O(1) time and space for fixed-width integers, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum product of at least two positive integers that sum to n.
Idea: Use dynamic programming over every total and possible first part.
Technique and why it applies: For each i, dp[i] compares j*(i-j) with j*dp[i-j] for j through half of i.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the best product for splitting i into at least two parts.
Edge cases: The recurrence handles small n through the initialized dp[1], but integerBreak inputs normally start at two.
Complexity: O(n^2) time and O(n) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize the product when n is split into at least two positive integers.
Idea: Use a rolling four-entry DP based on reducing the total by two or three.
Technique and why it applies: For n>=4, each state takes the better of the previous result times two or three, stored by index modulo four.
Invariant: The recurrence exploits that optimal decompositions can be extended by a factor of two or three.
Edge cases: n below four returns n-1 directly; the fixed ring retains the required earlier states.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum product from splitting n into positive integer parts.
Idea: Use the mathematical pattern of threes, with a remainder represented by zero, one, or two twos.
Technique and why it applies: For n>=4, the code chooses a power of three and multiplies by one, two, or four according to n modulo three.
Invariant: Replacing parts of four or more with smaller parts can increase the product, yielding the 3s-and-2s structure.
Edge cases: Small n returns n-1, ensuring at least two parts.
Complexity: O(log n) multiplications for exponentiation under a standard model, and O(1) auxiliary space; no time label supplied.

Task and constraints: Reverse a mutable character list in place.
Idea: Repeatedly pop the final element and insert it at the current index.
Technique and why it applies: For every index i, s.pop() removes the last character and s.insert(i,...) places it at the front portion.
Invariant: After enough rotations, the list appears reversed, but each insertion shifts elements.
Edge cases: The input list is mutated; the return value is that same list.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) due to repeated insert shifts, with O(1) extra space. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Reverse only the vowels in a string while leaving consonants in their original positions.
Idea: Collect vowels, reverse that list, and refill the marked positions.
Technique and why it applies: The code replaces vowel positions with '_', reverses vow, then fills each marker from the reversed vowel sequence.
Invariant: The non-vowel characters stay in place while vowel order is reversed.
Edge cases: It prints the vowel list as debug output; marker replacement assumes '_' cannot appear in input. The result is a new string.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for lists; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Reverse vowels in a string while preserving all other character positions.
Idea: Use two pointers to find vowels from opposite ends and swap them.
Technique and why it applies: The string is converted to a list; non-vowels advance one pointer, and vowel pairs are swapped before both pointers move inward.
Invariant: The section outside the two pointers is already finalized, with vowels reversed across the center.
Edge cases: Case-insensitive checks support uppercase vowels; the input string itself is immutable.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) extra list space, so the author O(1) space label excludes the converted output-sized list.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent values in an integer array.
Idea: Use Counter.most_common(k) and extract the keys from the top entries.
Technique and why it applies: Counter builds frequencies and most_common orders/selects the k highest-frequency entries.
Invariant: The returned keys correspond to the largest counts in the frequency table.
Edge cases: Ties may be returned in any order allowed by the API; Counter is not imported in the snippet.
Complexity: Expected O(n + u log k) time and O(u) space for u distinct values; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent values.
Idea: Count frequencies, then use randomized quickselect to partition frequency-key pairs around rank k-1.
Technique and why it applies: The code stores (-count,key) pairs, partitions them, then returns the first k keys from the partially ordered list.
Invariant: The partition ensures the selected side contains the k entries with highest frequencies, though internal order is not sorted.
Edge cases: Random pivoting gives expected linear selection; the returned order need not be frequency-sorted.
Complexity: Expected O(n+u) time after counting and O(u) space, worst-case selection O(u^2). No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the k values with highest frequencies.
Idea: Delegate counting and top-k extraction to Counter.most_common(k).
Technique and why it applies: The method creates a Counter and returns the keys from its k most common entries.
Invariant: Frequency order determines which keys are selected; exact ordering among ties depends on Counter behavior.
Edge cases: k is within the valid range under problem assumptions; Counter is explicitly imported.
Complexity: Expected O(n+u log k) time and O(u) space; the author O(n log k) label omits the linear counting cost but is a coarse upper bound for k>=1.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent elements using frequency buckets.
Idea: Group values by their occurrence count and scan buckets from highest frequency downward.
Technique and why it applies: The code creates buckets indexed by count, appends each distinct value to its count bucket, and collects values until k are found.
Invariant: A value in a higher bucket is more frequent than any value in a lower bucket.
Edge cases: The result may contain ties in arbitrary order; bucket count is bounded by nums length.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the distinct intersection of two integer arrays.
Idea: Sort both arrays and use two pointers to find equal values.
Technique and why it applies: The pointers advance on the smaller side; equal values are appended only if they differ from the last output, then both pointers advance.
Invariant: Sorting aligns equal values and the duplicate guard ensures each common value appears once.
Edge cases: Both input lists are sorted in place, so the original order is changed.
Complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time and O(1) extra space beyond sort internals/output; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the multiset intersection, preserving duplicate counts shared by both arrays.
Idea: Sort both lists and advance two pointers, appending each equal pair once.
Technique and why it applies: When current values match, append the value and advance both pointers; otherwise advance the pointer with the smaller value.
Invariant: Each matched occurrence consumes one occurrence from each array, so duplicates appear the minimum number of times.
Edge cases: Inputs are mutated by sorting; unmatched values are skipped.
Complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond sorting/output. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of envelopes that can be nested by increasing width and height.
Idea: Sort widths ascending and heights descending for ties, then find an increasing subsequence of heights.
Technique and why it applies: bisect_left finds the first tail at least as large as each height; replace that tail or append if height exceeds all tails.
Invariant: Descending heights for equal widths prevents envelopes of equal width from extending the subsequence.
Edge cases: The sorted copy avoids mutating the original envelopes list; equal heights do not extend strict LIS.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count non-negative integers with unique digits for numbers having at most n digits.
Idea: Use a recurrence for the number of valid choices at each digit length.
Technique and why it applies: table[0]=1, table[1]=9, and each later count multiplies the previous count by 11-i; the result sums all lengths.
Invariant: Each added digit has fewer unused choices than the previous digit.
Edge cases: n=0 returns one for number zero; the recurrence assumes the usual small n bound for this problem.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space. No author labels supplied.
